newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank officials boost sagging dollar.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank officials boost sagging dollar.

text.p: Top Bundesbank officials on Tuesday joined forces to help guide the U.S. dollar higher pushing the currency back above the psychologically key 1.50 marks level.

Bundesbank directorate member Edgar Meister told journalists in Mainz that the dollar was trading at "inappropriate" levels as it dipped below the 1.50 marks level, a long way off the 1.54 marks level seen in October.
And Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer in Frankfurt added later, "I always welcome it when the dollar finds it correct value," noting the currency was already climbing again.

While the Bundesbank insists it does not conduct a foreign exchange policy, there is little doubt that Bundesbank officials prefer to see the dollar above the 1.50 level, not below, as a lower rate hurts German exports and the economy.

After Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer this summer surprised markets with hints that rates could still be cut at precisely the time the dollar dipped below 1.50 marks, analysts also said a stronger dollar helped German monetary policy.

At the same time both Bundesbank officials hammered home Germany's strong objection to accounting adjustments being adopted by some nations as a last-ditch move to pass strict entry criteria to Europe's currency union.

Leaving no doubt he disapproved of what some officials have termed 'creative' accounting measures to help smooth over fiscal problems, Tietmeyer said,"I view certain beauty operations with worry as they are clearly designed to improve the finances for the appointed date."
"One-time efforts are not appropriate to create the necessary trust in the Euro," Tietmeyer warned in a speech delivered to foreign bankers in Frankfurt.

Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister, speaking to bankers in the city of Mainz, warned "creative accounting and one-off measures must be ruled out," even in the preliminary stages where nations' qualifications for the union are determined.

Recently, nations have stepped up their efforts to consolidate finances in order to be among the first nations to enter the currency union at the end of the decade, sometimes resorting to methods of unusual transfers.
France, for example will be able to use funds from a transfer from France Telekom to reduce its 1997 budget deficit. Its plans have been officially approved by the European Commission.

Although Bundesbank officials have declined to comment specifically on France's plans, both Tietmeyer and Meister warned such adjustments fail to meet the spirit of the Maastricht Treaty which calls for true convergence. Such moves only undermined trust in the new currency, they said.
"It is absolutely necessary that only nations with a convergent stability policy and sufficiently solid public finances can enter the currency union," Tietmeyer said.
To ensure lasting stability the officials also supported a stability pact, a German invention which seeks to punish nations who stray in fiscal austerity.

Separately, Tietmeyer also raised hopes the German central bank may agree to adjust its minimum reserve policy by exempting securities repurchase agreements from the requirement which may help improve Germany's status as a financial centre.
But Tietmeyer said the reserve requirement was essential to maintain stable monetary policy and that central bankers had largely agreed to adopt the concept for Europe's future central bank.
